Cyber Attack Disrupts Taiwan’s Real Estate Firms, Sites Remain Offline

TAIPEI – Multiple real estate firms across Taiwan are grappling with a major cyber attack that has left business platforms offline and disrupted operations for staff and agents. The incident, believed to be a ransomware assault, began early Thursday morning and is ongoing at the time of reporting, according to the Taiwan Real Estate Brokers Association.

The attack has forced the shutdown of internal IT systems at several of Taiwan’s largest brokerages, including Lianxin Realty and New Asia Estates. Company websites, email servers, and online property listing portals remain inaccessible. Employees were instructed to cease all digital transactions and avoid logging into company networks. As a result, property searches, online client communications, and digital document processing have been brought to a halt.

“It’s a severe situation. We have suspended all online operations to contain the breach,” said Chen Wei-chung, spokesperson for Lianxin Realty. “Our agents are unable to access listings or process contracts. We are working with cybersecurity experts to resolve the situation, but we do not have a timeline yet.”

For many property agents and support staff, the disruption has meant a sudden shift to manual processes or, in some cases, temporary suspension of work. “Our offices are unusually quiet,” said Lin Shu-ting, a leasing manager at New Asia Estates. “Without access to our database or email, our agents cannot confirm appointments or update property availability. Clients are frustrated, and we can only apologize.”

The Taiwan Real Estate Brokers Association estimated that over 40 percent of registered firms’ digital platforms are currently affected. “This is one of the most significant cyber incidents the industry has faced,” Association chairperson Huang Yu-feng stated. “Firms are prioritizing containment and recovery, but the attack’s full impact is not yet clear.”

Analysts warn that prolonged downtime could have lasting effects for agents and clients alike. “The inability to process transactions or access property data could lead to backlogs and revenue losses,” said Yang Hsin-ju, an independent IT security consultant.

Taipei police cybercrime units have launched an investigation, but no ransom demands have been confirmed publicly. As the situation develops, real estate professionals across Taiwan remain in limbo, awaiting restoration of their digital tools and services.
